nameStory: This millipede's scientific name 'caeruleocinctus' means 'blue-banded' in Latin, referring to the distinctive bluish bands that ring its cylindrical body segments. Like other barrel millipedes, it gets its common name from its rounded, barrel-like shape when viewed from the side, quite different from the flatter appearance of centipedes.
description: The Blue-banded Barrel Millipede is a small, cylindrical arthropod that looks like a tiny, segmented worm with many legs. It typically grows to about half an inch to an inch long, with a dark brown or blackish body marked by subtle bluish bands around each segment. Unlike centipedes which are predators, this millipede is a gentle decomposer that feeds on decaying plant matter. When disturbed, it curls up into a tight spiral like a tiny armadillo.

idTips.label: Cylindrical Shape
idTips.description: Body is perfectly round in cross-section, like a tiny smooth tube, rather than flattened like a centipede. Roll it gently between your fingers to feel its barrel-like roundness.

idTips.label: Bluish Bands
idTips.description: Look closely for faint blue or blue-gray bands or spots around each body segment. These may be subtle and show best in good lighting against the dark brown background.

idTips.label: Two Pairs of Legs per Segment
idTips.description: Each body segment has four tiny legs (two pairs), giving it a forest of legs underneath. Move slowly and deliberately, not with the quick darting movements of centipedes.

idTips.label: Defensive Coiling
idTips.description: When touched, immediately rolls into a tight spiral or ball, tucking its head inside. Feels smooth and hard when coiled, like a tiny pill bug but more tightly wound.

idTips.label: Size and Texture
idTips.description: About the thickness of a pencil lead to small straw, with a smooth, slightly shiny surface that feels firm but not slimy. Much smaller than earthworms found in the same habitat.

habitat: Found in moist soil, leaf litter, and decomposing organic matter throughout New England's forests and gardens. Look under logs, rocks, mulch, and compost piles where the soil stays consistently damp. Prefers areas with rich, organic soil and is often found alongside earthworms and other soil-dwelling invertebrates.

seasonality.spring: Active as soil warms up, often found when turning over winter debris and mulch in gardens. Look for them in compost piles and under logs where snow has recently melted.
seasonality.summer: Most active during humid weather and after rain showers. Best found by carefully lifting logs and rocks in shaded, moist areas during cooler morning or evening hours.
seasonality.fall: Very active as they feed on abundant fallen leaves and prepare for winter. Often discovered when raking leaves or moving garden debris to compost areas.
seasonality.winter: Dormant in deeper soil layers and protected spaces. Occasionally found in basement window wells or under deep mulch during mild winter days.

funFact: This European millipede hitchhiked to North America, likely in soil around imported plants, and has now become so widespread that it's found from coast to coast - a tiny immigrant success story that happened largely unnoticed under our feet!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with small earthworms, but millipedes have visible legs and coil up when touched while earthworms stretch and contract. Remember: 'Millipedes make spirals, earthworms make waves.' Also distinguished from centipedes by being slower, rounder, and having two pairs of legs per segment instead of one pair.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name suggesting 1,000 legs, this millipede actually has far fewer - typically 30-90 legs depending on how many segments it has developed. The 'milli' prefix is more about the appearance of having countless tiny legs rather than an actual count.
compareHints: Very similar to its relative the Blunt-tailed Snake Millipede, but the Blue-banded species shows those characteristic bluish markings around each segment while the Blunt-tailed tends to be more uniformly dark. Both are barrel-shaped and coil when disturbed, but the blue banding is the key distinguishing feature when present and visible.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The blunt-tailed snake millipede is distinguished from its relative Cylindroiulus caeruleocinctus by its distinctly blunt rear end and typically darker coloration.
